claim: Drug-resistant variants of positive-strand RNA viruses are generated due to error-prone replication of parental, drug-susceptible genomes.
source: Drug-resistant variants of positive-strand RNA viruses are generated due to error-prone replication of parental, drug-susceptible genomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of drug resistance emergence in RNA viruses, supported by established scientific knowledge about RNA virus replication fidelity.

claim: Error rates of 1 × 10−4 per nucleotide or higher ensure that each cell will experience a mixed infection as variant progeny genomes arise within it.
source: Even if individual host cells are infected with only a single virus each, error rates of 1 × 10−4 per nucleotide or higher ensure that each cell will experience a mixed infection as variant progeny genomes arise within it (Holland et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holland et al., 1989, which provides evidence for the error rates and their consequences.

claim: Guanidine treatment caused significant reductions in total viral yield in Tnfr1+/+ PVR+/+ mice after 4 days of viral infection.
source: Guanidine treatment caused significant reductions in total viral yield in Tnfr1+/+ PVR+/+ mice after 4 days of viral infection (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, which displays viral yields in treated vs. untreated mice.

claim: Guanidine treatment caused significant reductions in total viral yield in Tnfr1−/− PVR+/+ mice after 5 days of infection.
source: Guanidine treatment caused significant reductions in total viral yield in Tnfr1+/+ PVR+/+ mice after 4 days of viral infection (Figure 1B) and in Tnfr1−/− PVR+/+ mice after 5 days of infection (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Large and significant increases in the frequency of guanidine resistance were observed in all guanidine-treated mice.
source: Large and significant increases in the frequency of guanidine resistance were observed in all treated mice (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1E.

claim: Guanidine-resistant variants naturally occur at a frequency of approximately two in one thousand.
source: Due to the heterogeneous nature of the viral population, even samples from untreated mice contain a measureable background frequency of guanidine-resistant variants. These variants naturally occur at a frequency of approximately two in one thousand.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from untreated control mice in the experiments.

claim: V-073 treatment caused a significant decrease in viral titer after 4, 5 and 7 days of infection.
source: V-073 treatment caused a significant decrease in viral titer after 4, 5 and 7 days of infection (Figure 1F,H, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F, 1H, and 1J.

claim: No increase in the frequency of V-073 resistance was observed at any time point during V-073 treatment.
source: However, no increase in the frequency of V-073 resistance was observed at any time point (Figure 1G,I, K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G, 1I, and 1K.

claim: V-073-resistant variants naturally occurred at a frequency of approximately one in ten thousand in samples from untreated mice.
source: Both guanidine- and V-073-resistant variants naturally occurred at a frequency of approximately one in ten thousand in samples from untreated mice.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from untreated control mice in the experiments.

claim: Guanidine-resistant viruses were viable but displayed significantly reduced fitness compared to wild-type virus in mice.
source: When these stocks were used to infect mice (Figure 2A), the guanidine-resistant viruses were viable but displayed significantly reduced fitness compared to wild-type virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A comparing viral yields.

claim: Only a slight and statistically insignificant difference in fitness between wild-type virus and the V-073-resistant virus stock was observed.
source: On the other hand, only a slight and statistically insignificant difference in fitness between wild-type virus and the V-073-resistant virus stock was observed.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data comparing viral yields.

claim: Fitness costs do not account for the lack of outgrowth of V-073-resistant virus.
source: Therefore, we conclude that fitness costs do not account for the lack of outgrowth of V-073-resistant virus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that V-073-resistant viruses have similar fitness to wild-type but still don't emerge during treatment.

claim: WIN compounds have sixty binding sites on each picornavirus virion.
source: For several picornaviruses, the function of viral capsid can be inhibited by 'WIN' compounds, which have sixty binding sites on each virion (Diana et al., 1985; Smith et al., 1986)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Diana et al., 1985 and Smith et al., 1986.

claim: WIN compound binding sites are hydrophobic pockets arrayed about each of the twelve fivefold axes.
source: These binding sites are hydrophobic pockets arrayed about each of the twelve fivefold axes (Diana et al., 1985; Smith et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Diana et al., 1985 and Smith et al., 1986.

claim: Drug binding reduces capsid flexibility thereby preventing the conformational changes required for cell entry and capsid uncoating.
source: Drug binding reduces capsid flexibility thereby preventing the conformational changes required for cell entry and capsid uncoating (Lewis et al., 1998; Dove and Racaniello, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lewis et al., 1998 and Dove and Racaniello, 2000.

claim: V-073 inhibits all three poliovirus serotypes.
source: A chemically related drug, V-073, inhibits all three poliovirus serotypes and is currently in clinical development (Buontempo et al., 1997; Collett et al., 2008; Oberste et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buontempo et al., 1997; Collett et al., 2008; and Oberste et al., 2009.

claim: V-073 is currently in clinical development.
source: A chemically related drug, V-073, inhibits all three poliovirus serotypes and is currently in clinical development (Buontempo et al., 1997; Collett et al., 2008; Oberste et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buontempo et al., 1997; Collett et al., 2008; and Oberste et al., 2009.

claim: Tnfr1−/− PVR+/+ mice displayed reduced pathogenesis compared to Tnfr1+/+ PVR+/+ mice.
source: This is in contrast to Tnfr1−/− PVR+/+ mice, which displayed reduced pathogenesis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The yield of total virus after 4 days of infection was higher in Tnfr1+/+ mice than in Tnfr1−/− mice.
source: When testing drug resistance in Tnfr1+/+ mice, the yield of total virus after 4 days of infection was higher than in Tnfr1−/− mice (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment of poliovirus-infected transgenic mice with guanidine throughout a course of infection did not affect pathogenesis.
source: Treatment of poliovirus-infected transgenic mice with guanidine throughout a course of infection did not affect pathogenesis (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In mice that developed poliomyelitis during guanidine treatment, large and significant increases in the frequency of guanidine-resistant virus were observed.
source: However, the compound certainly had some effect: in mice that developed poliomyelitis, large and significant increases in the frequency of guanidine-resistant virus were observed (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: When mice developed paralysis during V-073-treatment, no selection for V-073-resistant virus was seen.
source: On the other hand, when the few mice that developed paralysis during V-073-treatment were analyzed, no selection for V-073-resistant virus was seen (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The 2C-N179G mutation confers complete resistance to 0.5 mM guanidine.
source: For guanidine (Figure 3A), a known variant, 2C-N179G (Pincus and Wimmer, 1986), was reconstructed and shown to confer complete resistance to 0.5 mM guanidine (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Pincus and Wimmer, 1986.

claim: The yield of guanidine-resistant virus in the presence of the drug was the same whether susceptible viruses were present or not.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, the yield of guanidine-resistant virus in the presence of the drug was the same whether susceptible viruses were present or not.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Even when the guanidine-resistant variant was outnumbered 100:1, its growth was unimpeded by the presence of wild-type, drug-susceptible virus.
source: Even when the guanidine-resistant variant was outnumbered 100:1, its growth was unimpeded by the presence of wild-type, drug-susceptible virus (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Targeting the viral NTPase with guanidine allows the growth of drug-resistant genomes even in the presence of an excess of drug-susceptible ones.
source: Therefore, targeting the viral NTPase with guanidine allows the growth of drug-resistant genomes even in the presence of an excess of drug-susceptible ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-infection experiments with guanidine.

claim: Co-infection of wild-type, drug-susceptible virus with V-073 resistant virus resulted in a dominant inhibition in drug-resistant virus growth.
source: Unlike with guanidine, co-infection of wild-type, drug-susceptible virus with V-073 resistant virus resulted in a dominant inhibition in drug-resistant virus growth (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The dominant inhibition of V-073-resistant virus did not result from the decreased fitness of V-073-resistant virus.
source: As in mice, this did not result from the decreased fitness of V-073-resistant virus (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H showing similar growth in the absence of drug.

claim: Even at only a fivefold excess of V-073-susceptible virus, the yield of drug-resistant virus was reduced by 98%.
source: Even at only a fivefold excess of V-073-susceptible virus, the yield of drug-resistant virus was reduced by 98%.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of the co-infection experimental data.

claim: The Hispaniola strain of vaccine-derived neurovirulent poliovirus is known to be susceptible to V-073.
source: To determine whether selection for V-073-resistant virus was also suppressed in a viral strain isolated from a poliomyelitis patient (Kew et al., 2002), we tested whether the Hispaniola strain of vaccine-derived neurovirulent poliovirus, known to be susceptible to V-073 (Oberste et al., 2009), was dominant over two different V-073-resistant variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oberste et al., 2009.

claim: The VP3-A24V mutation alters residues that line the pocket known to bind V-073.
source: One such variant harbored the VP3-A24V mutation mentioned above and the second contained an I194F mutation in another capsid protein, VP1 (Kouiavskaia et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012). Each of these mutations alters residues that line the pocket known to bind V-073, confers drug resistance and allows growth comparable to wild-type virus in the absence of drug (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kouiavskaia et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2012.

claim: The VP1-I194F mutation alters residues that line the pocket known to bind V-073.
source: One such variant harbored the VP3-A24V mutation mentioned above and the second contained an I194F mutation in another capsid protein, VP1 (Kouiavskaia et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012). Each of these mutations alters residues that line the pocket known to bind V-073, confers drug resistance and allows growth comparable to wild-type virus in the absence of drug (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kouiavskaia et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2012.

claim: The VP3-A24V and VP1-I194F mutations confer drug resistance and allow growth comparable to wild-type virus in the absence of drug.
source: Each of these mutations alters residues that line the pocket known to bind V-073, confers drug resistance and allows growth comparable to wild-type virus in the absence of drug (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3I and 3J.

claim: V-073-resistant Hispaniola-derived variants were profoundly inhibited by the presence of the parental strain.
source: Like the laboratory-passaged Mahoney type 1 strain (Figure 3G), these V-073-resistant Hispaniola-derived variants were profoundly inhibited by the presence of the parental strain (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3K and 3L.

claim: Drug-susceptible virus was genetically dominant over drug-resistant variants in both lab-passaged and disease-causing strains.
source: Therefore, drug-susceptible virus was genetically dominant over drug-resistant variants in both lab-passaged and disease-causing strains, suggesting that V-073 is a general dominant drug target inhibitor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing Mahoney and Hispaniola strains.

claim: Rupintrivir is an active site inhibitor of enterovirus 3C proteinases.
source: Rupintrivir (Figure 3M) is an active site inhibitor of enterovirus 3C proteinases (Patick et al., 1999, 2005; Wang et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Patick et al., 1999, 2005 and Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Rupintrivir is the most effective inhibitor of poliovirus growth tested in cell culture.
source: Rupintrivir (Figure 3M) is an active site inhibitor of enterovirus 3C proteinases (Patick et al., 1999, 2005; Wang et al., 2011), and is, in cell culture, the most effective inhibitor of poliovirus growth tested here (Figure 3N).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data from the different inhibitors tested.

claim: The phenotype of the rupintrivir-resistant variant was caused by a single amino acid change, G128Q, in the 3C coding region.
source: The phenotype of the rupintrivir-resistant variant (Figure 3N) was caused by a single amino acid change, G128Q, in the 3C coding region.
evidence: This claim is based on sequencing data and genetic reconstruction experiments.

claim: The yield of rupintrivir-resistant virus grown in the presence of rupintrivir was relatively unperturbed by the presence of susceptible virus.
source: As was the case with guanidine, the yield of rupintrivir-resistant virus grown in the presence of rupintrivir was relatively unperturbed by the presence of susceptible virus (Figure 3O), up to ratios of 100:1 of susceptible to resistant virus (Figure 3P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3O and 3P.

claim: Viral proteinase 3C is a non-dominant drug target.
source: Thus, viral proteinase 3C, like viral NTPase 2C, is a non-dominant drug target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-infection experiments with rupintrivir.

claim: The lack of infectivity of virions made in V-073-treated cells is due to the formation of chimeric capsids.
source: We hypothesized that the lack of infectivity of virions made in V-073-treated cells was due to the formation of chimeric capsids (Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is then tested experimentally.

claim: FLAG-tagged virus retained its V-073-resistant phenotype in single-cycle infections.
source: In single-cycle infections, the FLAG-tagged virus retained its V-073-resistant phenotype, and the HA-tagged virus its drug susceptibility (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HA-tagged virus retained its drug susceptibility in single-cycle infections.
source: In single-cycle infections, the FLAG-tagged virus retained its V-073-resistant phenotype, and the HA-tagged virus its drug susceptibility (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Anti-FLAG immunoprecipitation of lysates from single infections retrieved FLAG-tagged drug-resistant but not HA-tagged drug-susceptible virus.
source: Anti-FLAG immunoprecipitation of lysates obtained from these single infections retrieved, as expected, FLAG-tagged drug-resistant but not HA-tagged drug-susceptible virus (Figure 4E) or proteins (Figure 4F, lanes 1 and 2, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: When two lysates were pooled, only FLAG-tagged, V-073-resistant virus was recovered by anti-FLAG immunoprecipitation.
source: When the two lysates were pooled, only FLAG-tagged, V-073-resistant virus was recovered (Figure 4E,F, lane 3), demonstrating that the immunoprecipitation was specific for capsids harboring proteins from the V-073-resistant genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E and 4F, lane 3.

claim: When drug-resistant, FLAG-tagged virus and drug-susceptible HA-tagged virus were co-infected into cells, the anti-FLAG immunoprecipitated virions displayed reduced infectivity when soaked in the capsid inhibitor prior to titering.
source: When the drug-resistant, FLAG-tagged virus and the drug-susceptible HA-tagged virus were co-infected into cells and the anti-FLAG immunoprecipitation was performed, the immunoprecipitated virions displayed reduced infectivity when soaked in the capsid inhibitor prior to titering (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The anti-FLAG immunoprecipitate from co-infected cells contained both FLAG- and HA-tagged VP1 proteins.
source: Furthermore, the anti-FLAG immunoprecipitate contained both FLAG- and HA-tagged VP1 proteins (Figure 4F, lane 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F, lane 4.

claim: Chimeric virions with reduced drug resistance were formed in cells co-infected with V-073 susceptible and V-073-resistant viruses.
source: Therefore, chimeric virions with reduced drug-resistance were formed in cells co-infected with V-073 susceptible and V-073-resistant viruses, even at the 1:1 ratio tested here.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunoprecipitation experiments showing both tagged proteins in the same virions with reduced drug resistance.

claim: The formation of mixed capsids with reduced drug resistance is the most plausible explanation for the observed genetic dominance of V-073-susceptible variants.
source: The formation of mixed capsids with reduced drug resistance is the most plausible explanation for the observed genetic dominance of V-073-susceptible variants and the blunted selection for drug-resistance during growth in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental evidence.

claim: Any stock of lab-passaged 'wild-type' virus contains pre-existing drug-resistant variants.
source: Similar to the heterogeneity observed in virus stocks from mouse muscles, any stock of lab-passaged 'wild-type' virus contains pre-existing drug-resistant variants.
evidence: This is based on the known high mutation rate of RNA viruses and observations from the experiments.

claim: When HeLa cells were infected at an MOI of 1 infectious virus per cell in the presence of either guanidine or V-073, the yields of guanidine-resistant and V-073-resistant viruses were similar.
source: Consistent with this logic, when HeLa cells were infected at an MOI of 1 infectious virus per cell in the presence of either guanidine or V-073, the yields of guanidine-resistant and V-073-resistant viruses were similar (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At higher MOIs, the yield of guanidine-resistant progeny increased.
source: At higher MOIs, the yield of guanidine-resistant progeny increased, as would be expected because more virus was present in the inoculum and nothing interfered with the outgrowth of the drug-resistant variants (Figure 5C, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The yield of V-073-resistant progeny decreased at high MOIs.
source: However, the yield of V-073-resistant progeny decreased at high MOIs (Figure 5B and Figure 5C, orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: When the virus stock was soaked in V-073 before infections at different MOIs, a dose-dependent increase in the yield of V-073-resistant virus was observed even at high MOIs.
source: When entry of the drug-susceptible viruses was thus inhibited, a dose-dependent increase in the yield of V-073-resistant virus was observed even at high MOIs (Figure 5C, dotted orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Failure to select V-073-resistant genomes at high MOIs could be overcome by preventing the entry of the drug-susceptible genomes.
source: Thus, failure to select V-073-resistant genomes at high MOIs could be overcome by preventing the entry of the drug-susceptible genomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pretreatment experiments.

claim: A single inhibitor of a positive-strand RNA virus, capsid poison V-073, can both inhibit viral growth and suppress the emergence of newly arising drug-resistant variants during infection of mice and of cultured cells.
source: In this study we have shown that a single inhibitor of a positive-strand RNA virus, capsid poison V-073, can both inhibit viral growth and suppress the emergence of newly arising drug-resistant variants during infection of mice and of cultured cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The formation of chimeric capsids, which contained both drug-inhibitable and drug-resistant proteins, correlated with the suppression of drug resistance.
source: Deliberate mixed infections performed in cell culture showed that the formation of chimeric capsids, which contained both drug-inhibitable and drug-resistant proteins, correlated with the suppression of drug resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the immunoprecipitation experiments and co-infection studies.

claim: Targeting the viral constituents of an oligomeric assemblage, such as a viral capsid, can lead to the genetic dominance of drug-susceptible genomes.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that targeting the viral constituents of an oligomeric assemblage, such as a viral capsid, can lead to the genetic dominance of drug-susceptible genomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: For poliovirus in this mouse model, more than 104 viruses are required to achieve any detectable viral growth in muscle tissue.
source: For poliovirus in this mouse model, more than 104 viruses are required to achieve any detectable viral growth in muscle tissue (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished experimental data.

claim: V-073 was effective at suppressing resistance even as a monotherapy because V-073-susceptible variants suppress the growth of V-073-resistant variants as they arise intracellularly throughout the course of infection.
source: Therefore, we conclude that V-073 was effective at suppressing resistance even as a monotherapy because V-073-susceptible variants suppress the growth of V-073-resistant variants as they arise intracellularly throughout the course of infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and the dominant drug target mechanism.

claim: A delay in treatment will not alter the degree to which dominant drug target inhibitors suppress the selection of newly arising resistant viral genomes from drug-susceptible parents.
source: However, a delay in treatment will not alter the degree to which dominant drug target inhibitors suppress the selection of newly arising resistant viral genomes from drug-susceptible parents.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of dominant drug targeting.

claim: Trans-encapsidation of newly arising drug-resistant genomes by the intracellular excess of drug-susceptible capsids should provide an additional mechanism to reduce the reservoir of drug-resistant genomes packaged in drug-resistant capsids.
source: Thus, for a capsid inhibitor, trans-encapsidation of newly arising drug-resistant genomes by the intracellular excess of drug-susceptible capsids should provide an additional mechanism to reduce the reservoir of drug-resistant genomes packaged in drug-resistant capsids.
evidence: This is a logical inference about an additional mechanism based on the dominant drug target concept.

claim: The use of dominant drug targets is expected to reduce the number of antiviral compounds necessary for effective treatment of individuals and populations.
source: The use of dominant drug targets is expected to reduce the number of antiviral compounds necessary for effective treatment of individuals and populations.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: There has been hesitation to use V-073 as a monotherapy.
source: In the case of V-073, the only poliovirus antiviral currently in human trials, there has been hesitation to use it as a monotherapy (Collett et al., 2008; De Palma et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Collett et al., 2008 and De Palma et al., 2008.

claim: V-073 may be sufficient for the effective treatment of poliovirus infection.
source: Our data suggest that V-073 may be sufficient for the effective treatment of poliovirus infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing suppression of resistance.

claim: The most direct way for a drug-susceptible virus to be genetically dominant over a drug-resistant one is the formation of mixed oligomers.
source: The most direct way for a drug-susceptible virus to be genetically dominant over a drug-resistant one is the formation of mixed oligomers, as exemplified here.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and mechanistic understanding.

claim: Co-transfection experiments identified the viral capsid and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase as viral products whose fitness could be suppressed by the presence of defective subunits.
source: For poliovirus, co-transfection experiments identified known oligomers such as the viral capsid and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase as viral products whose fitness could be suppressed by the presence of defective subunits (Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005.

claim: Intramolecularly cleaving protease 2A was identified as a potential dominant drug target.
source: Other candidates also emerged, however, whose mechanisms are less straightforward and remain under investigation: intramolecularly cleaving protease 2A and an RNA structure required for protein priming were also identified as potential dominant drug targets (Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005.

claim: An RNA structure required for protein priming was identified as a potential dominant drug target.
source: Other candidates also emerged, however, whose mechanisms are less straightforward and remain under investigation: intramolecularly cleaving protease 2A and an RNA structure required for protein priming were also identified as potential dominant drug targets (Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005.

claim: All dominant drug targets should share a unique feature: binding of the drug to its target generates a product that is toxic to the drug-resistant variant.
source: All dominant drug targets should share a unique feature: binding of the drug to its target generates a product that is toxic to the drug-resistant variant.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Three factors are required for dominant drug targeting: 1) The drug-bound product must interact with proteins made by the drug-resistant genome; 2) the interaction between drug-bound products and resistant proteins must inhibit an essential step in the infectious cycle of the virus; and 3) the ratio of drug-susceptible to drug-resistant products synthesized in the cell must be high enough to poison the function of the resistant variant.
source: Three factors are required to accomplish this effect. 1) The drug-bound product must interact with proteins made by the drug-resistant genome; 2) the interaction between drug-bound products and resistant proteins must inhibit an essential step in the infectious cycle of the virus; and 3) the ratio of drug-susceptible to drug-resistant products synthesized in the cell must be high enough to poison the function of the resistant variant.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework proposed based on the experimental findings and mechanistic understanding.

claim: Small-molecule screens are often designed to detect loss of viral product function, rather than the deranged function required for the drug-bound, susceptible viral product to join and poison drug-resistant complexes.
source: Small-molecule screens are often designed to detect loss of viral product function, rather than the deranged function required for the drug-bound, susceptible viral product to join and poison drug-resistant complexes.
evidence: This is a statement about current drug screening practices based on general knowledge of the field.

claim: V-073 hyper-stabilizes viral capsids.
source: V-073, for example, hyper-stabilizes viral capsids.
evidence: This is based on known properties of V-073 and related compounds.

claim: A theoretical capsid inhibitor that prevented assembly by binding at an intersubunit interface should display the characteristics of a non-dominant drug target inhibitor.
source: A theoretical capsid inhibitor that prevented assembly by binding at an intersubunit interface should display the characteristics of a non-dominant drug target inhibitor, because the drug-susceptible subunits would not have the opportunity to poison the drug-resistant subunits.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the mechanism of dominant drug targeting.

claim: Trans-assembly of highly oligomeric complexes is a hallmark of RNA viral infection.
source: Indeed, trans-assembly of highly oligomeric complexes is a hallmark of RNA viral infection, exemplified by the polymerase and polymerase-containing oligomers of positive-strand RNA viruses (Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005; Marcotte et al., 2007; Kemball et al., 2010) and the large nucleoprotein-RNA complexes that form during negative-strand RNA replication (Reviewed in reference Morin et al. (2013)).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: About twenty subunits, or one third, of the capsid proteins must be drug-susceptible to poison the complex.
source: Again using the poliovirus capsid as an example, we can calculate the approximate number of susceptible subunits required to render the entire virion drug-susceptible. Assuming free mixing of drug-susceptible and drug-resistant capsids and relative abundances that reflect the ratio of their genomes, the data argue that about twenty subunits, or one third, of the capsid proteins must be drug-susceptible to poison the complex.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data from co-infection experiments.

claim: V-073 would not have been detected as a viable inhibitor in a screen that used a decrease in genome amplification, protein abundance or innate immune response activation during a single cycle of infection as a proxy for viral inhibition.
source: V-073, for example, would not have been detected as a viable inhibitor in a screen that used a decrease in genome amplification, protein abundance or innate immune response activation during a single cycle of infection as a proxy for viral inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference about screening strategies based on the mechanism of action of V-073.

claim: Capsids, cores and other oligomeric assemblages of rhinovirus, enterovirus 71, hepatitis C and dengue virus are likely to be dominant drug targets.
source: Thus, capsids, cores and other oligomeric assemblages of rhinovirus, enterovirus 71, hepatitis C and dengue virus are likely to be dominant drug targets.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings with poliovirus and the similar biology of these viruses.

claim: The dominant drug targeting strategy may not apply to retroviruses, because the step with the least fidelity, reverse transcription, gives rise to a low copy number DNA intermediate.
source: This strategy may not apply to retroviruses, because the step with the least fidelity, reverse transcription, gives rise to a low copy number DNA intermediate.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the biology of retroviruses and the requirements for dominant drug targeting.

claim: Bona fide DNA viruses, present at a high copy number per cell, should be amenable to the dominant drug targeting strategy.
source: However, bona fide DNA viruses, present at a high copy number per cell, should also be amenable to this dominant drug targeting strategy.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the mechanism of dominant drug targeting.

claim: For other error-prone, intracellular genetic amplification events, such as the growth of bacterial and eukaryotic intracellular pathogens and the gene duplication associated with oncogenesis, the choice of oligomeric drug targets may also suppress the outgrowth of drug-resistant variants immediately after their inception.
source: For other error-prone, intracellular genetic amplification events, such as the growth of bacterial and eukaryotic intracellular pathogens and the gene duplication associated with oncogenesis, the choice of oligomeric drug targets may also suppress the outgrowth of drug-resistant variants immediately after their inception.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the dominant drug target concept to other biological systems.

claim: Deliberate targeting of oligomeric structures should reduce the numbers of inhibitors needed for effective treatment.
source: Deliberate targeting of oligomeric structures should reduce the numbers of inhibitors needed for effective treatment, but will require revision of decision-making processes during drug development.
evidence: This is a conclusion and recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Expression of a non-functional version of the oligomeric Tat protein of HIV drastically reduces viral yield.
source: Expression of a non-functional version of the oligomeric Tat protein of HIV drastically reduces viral yield (Meredith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Meredith et al., 2009.

claim: Co-expression of non-functional NS5A protein of hepatitis C virus inhibits replication of genomes that encode functional NS5A.
source: Similarly, co-expression of non-functional NS5A protein of hepatitis C virus inhibits replication of genomes that encode functional NS5A (Graziani and Paonessa, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Graziani and Paonessa, 2004.

claim: In poliovirus, viral genomes with mutations in several proteins, including capsid proteins and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, interfere with the amplification of co-transfected wild-type viral genomes.
source: In poliovirus, viral genomes with mutations in several proteins, including capsid proteins and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, interfere with the amplification of co-transfected wild-type viral genomes (Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crowder and Kirkegaard, 2005.

claim: V-073 is an inhibitor of viral capsid function that is currently in development for use in the poliovirus eradication campaign.
source: Here, we show that V-073, an inhibitor of viral capsid function that is currently in development for use in the poliovirus eradication campaign (Buontempo et al., 1997; Collett et al., 2008; Oberste et al., 2009), fulfills the expectations of dominant drug targeting
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buontempo et al., 1997; Collett et al., 2008; and Oberste et al., 2009.

claim: The NTPase activity of protein 2C is inhibited by low concentrations of guanidine in cell culture and in solution.
source: The NTPase activity of protein 2C is inhibited by low concentrations of guanidine in cell culture and in solution (Pfister and Wimmer, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pfister and Wimmer, 1999.

claim: V-073 is the only poliovirus antiviral currently in human trials.
source: In the case of V-073, the only poliovirus antiviral currently in human trials, there has been hesitation to use it as a monotherapy (Collett et al., 2008; De Palma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the context of discussing V-073's clinical development status.
